newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S. peace envoy says Hebron gaps bridgeable.
newsitem.headline: U.S. peace envoy says Hebron gaps bridgeable.

text.p: U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross, ending a three-week U.S. bid to win accord on an Israeli army pullout from the West Bank town of Hebron, said on Monday the gaps between Israel and the PLO were "very definitely brigeable."
Israel and the PLO blamed each other for the collapse on Monday of the U.S. mission to nail down a Hebron accord, but insisted that talks will go on in an effort to break a deadlock.
"We've made headway, we've narrowed the differences," Ross told reporters late on Monday. "I believe that the differences that exist right now are very definitely brigeable."
U.S. President Bill Clinton dispatched Ross to the region in the wake of unprecedented Palestinian-Israeli gun battles last month that left scores dead in the West Bank and Gaza.
The mission has since ridden a diplomatic roller-coaster of near-agreements and sudden crises. "I think that agreement is possible," Ross said. "We still have work to do to get it."
Ross announced he was leaving a week ago, only to be called back from the airport as new hope glimmered for agreement on the long-promised withdrawal. He was expected to leave overnight.

Israel's ambassador to Washington charged on Monday that Palestinian President Yasser Arafat had spurned an appeal by Ross to postpone a European trip in order to meet Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and seal a Hebron accord.
Arafat, in Oslo on the first leg of the three-day swing, said it was Israel that was keeping the deal from being struck.
"I am sorry to say that still the Israelis are making new conditions every day," Arafat said. He said agreement could still be reached on Hebron before U.S. elections on November 5.
Arafat rejected Israeli charges he was stalling on the accord for Hebron, the last of seven West Bank towns the Jewish state agreed to hand over to Palestinian self-rule.
Israel's previous Labour government agreed to a withdrawal from much of the violence-plagued town more than a year ago, but froze implementation during a wave of Islamic suicide bombings.

Palestinians accuse Israel of trying to dictate new terms for the Hebron redeployment, delayed since March. Israel has said adjustments are necessary to safeguard the 400 Jews who live under heavy army guard in the town of 100,000 Arabs.
The differences centred on Israel's demand for the right to pursue militants into parts of Hebron it hands over, and what arms PLO police would be allowed to carry, Palestinians said.
Both sides said talks would continue.
The Hebron impasse raised fears of fresh violence in the West Bank and Gaza, a month after raging gun battles claimed the lives of 60 Palestinians and 15 Israeli soldiers.
Hebron, cradle and rallying point of Jewish and Islamic militancy, was tense but quiet on Monday, but unrest threatened to resume in other areas.

Arab anger was stirred by the death of a 10-year-old Arab boy, who succumbed in hospital on Monday after being beaten in the West Bank by a Jewish settler who suspected he had thrown stones at Israeli cars, the boy's father said.
Israel's ties with its Arab neighbours have plunged to crisis levels since the hardline Netanyahu defeated Shimon Peres last May with a promise to go slow and get tough in peace talks.
Security sources said Netanyahu's defence chiefs have told him the army needed more than $1 billion because of an increased chance of war with Syria.
But Defense Minister Yitzhak Mordechai, appearing to depart from Netanyahu's unbending line, hinted Israel might cede some of the Golan Heights to Syria in return for peace.
The European Union moved to bolster its role in the peace process, naming a Middle East envoy and pointedly joining with Egypt in urging Israel to pull out of Hebron.
Clinton urged both Arafat and Netanyahu in separate telephone calls on Sunday to seal the deal.
